title: Khinchin's ergodicity and typicality in statistical mechanics
authors: Dario Lucente, Marco Baldovin, Giacomo Gradenigo, Angelo Vulpiani
abstract: The formulation of statistical mechanics in terms of ensembles, originally proposed by Gibbs, has proved to be extremely effective in describing the equilibrium state of many-particle systems, in the most diverse contexts (critical phenomena, quantum mechanics, biophysics, just to mention a few). The reasons of this success are still debated, and the connection between dynamics and probability in large systems remains somehow elusive. Indeed, in order to derive the main results of equilibrium statistical mechanics, strong assumptions on the ergodicity of the dynamics are usually required. Nonetheless, empirical observations seem to suggest that the predictions of the theory hold true even when such assumptions are not verified. In this paper we reconsider the point of view put forward by Khinchin, stating that the only relevant ingredients for the validity of statistical mechanics are the large number of degrees of freedom in the system and the choice of extensive observables, irrespectively of the details of the microscopic dynamics. In particular, the presence of dynamical chaos is not required. To this aim, we discuss some analytical and numerical results on a couple of classical integrable systems, the harmonic chain and the Toda model, showing that many important features predicted by equilibrium statistical mechanics, as for instance Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, are found even in absence of chaos.
summary: This paper re-examines the ergodic hypothesis, arguing that the success of statistical mechanics stems not from the dynamics being chaotic, but from the sheer number of degrees of freedom in the system. By analyzing integrable models like the Toda chain, the authors show that key thermodynamic distributions emerge robustly in the thermodynamic limit, weakening the strict requirement of ergodicity.
main_problem: The paper addresses the fundamental connection between time averages (dynamics) and phase averages (ensemble theory) in statistical mechanics, specifically challenging the necessity of the strong ergodic hypothesis.
main_result: Key predictions of equilibrium statistical mechanics, such as the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, can hold true even in classically integrable systems where strong ergodicity is violated, suggesting the role of the large number of degrees of freedom is paramount.
method: The authors use analytical derivations, asymptotic analysis of partition functions, and numerical simulations on integrable models to test the convergence of time averages to ensemble averages.
model_or_system: The analysis focuses on classical Hamiltonian systems, including the harmonic chain and the non-linear Toda model. These systems are used to test the ergodic hypothesis in the context of the thermodynamic limit ($N 	o \infty$).
key_observables: Time averages of observables, the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, the intensive quantity $y$ used to test typicality, and the specific heat.
important_parameters: The number of degrees of freedom ($N$), the temperature parameter ($ eta$), and the limit of large $N$.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is the validity of Khinchin's view: that statistical mechanics relies only on the large number of degrees of freedom and the choice of extensive observables, irrespective of chaotic dynamics.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the distribution of time averages (e.g., $w(t^*)$) collapsing onto a single curve as $N$ increases, and show the standard deviations of time averages of conserved quantities remaining small.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first defining the ergodic problem, then analyzing integrable systems (like the harmonic chain) to show expected distributions arise despite non-chaos, and finally applying this framework to the Toda model to demonstrate typicality in the thermodynamic limit.
why_interesting: It provides a deep theoretical underpinning for why equilibrium statistical mechanics works, suggesting that the failure of strict ergodicity does not invalidate macroscopic thermodynamic predictions in the large-$N$ limit.
